\chapter{Ser in the Plural}
\label{ch:spanish-ser-plural}
\hlchaptermodality{49}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use all six present forms of ser, and say why no two of them look alike.}

Two Latin verbs in one paradigm - and the seam between them is visible at eres.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[somos]{somos — \textquotedblleft{}we are\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C09-somos}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}I am.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Soy}.) And \textquotedblleft{}we speak.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Hablamos}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the -mos survives even here}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{somos} — \emph{we are.}
\end{quote}

Look at what survived. \emph{Ser} is the most irregular verb in Spanish — \emph{soy}, \emph{eres}, \emph{es} share almost nothing — and yet the plural still ends in \textbf{-mos}, exactly as \emph{hablamos} and \emph{comemos} do.

That ending is the single most stable thing in the language. Even a verb that has thrown away everything else kept it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
And here is why \emph{ser}'s forms refuse to resemble each other: \textbf{it is not one verb.} It is two Latin verbs fused into a single paradigm.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Latin \textbf{esse}, \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{}, gave \emph{soy} and \emph{somos} — the \emph{s-} forms, and the rest of that family arrives over the next two lessons.
  \item Latin \textbf{sedēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to sit\textquotedblright{}, gave \emph{ser} itself, and the future and conditional.
\end{itemize}

So \emph{somos} and \emph{ser} are not irregular versions of each other. They are descendants of \textbf{different words}, brought together because Spanish needed one verb where Latin had two.

English did something very similar. \emph{Am}, \emph{is}, \emph{are}, \emph{was}, \emph{be} — no two of those look related, because they are not: they come from three separate Old English verbs. Every language seems to build \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} out of spare parts.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}hablamos, comemos, somos\textquotedblright{} — the same ending, three times
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}we are\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Somos}.) Which ending did even this verb keep? (\textbf{-mos}.) And why do \emph{soy} and \emph{ser} look unrelated? (They \textbf{are} unrelated — two Latin verbs in one paradigm.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[son]{son — \textquotedblleft{}they are\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C09-son}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}we are.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Somos}.) And \textquotedblleft{}they speak.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Hablan}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the final -n, again}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{son} — \emph{they are}, and \textbf{ustedes son}, \emph{you all are}.
\end{quote}

Three letters, and it is one of the two or three commonest words in the whole language. The rule you know holds even here: a final \textbf{-n} means the subject is plural and is not you.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin's form was \textbf{sunt}. Spanish dropped the final \textbf{-t}, exactly as it dropped it from \emph{hablat} to give \emph{habla}, and \emph{sunt} became \emph{son}.

That is worth noticing because it is the same erosion you have already watched happen twice. Irregular verbs are not exempt from sound change; they are simply verbs where sound change ran on material that had already been strange.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{A word you may already know.} English \emph{sonata}, \emph{sonnet} and \emph{sound} have nothing to do with this — they come from Latin \emph{sonāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to sound\textquotedblright{}. \emph{Son} the verb and \emph{son} the noun in English are unrelated to each other and to both. Spanish is full of these collisions, and the way through is always the same: the root, not the spelling.
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}somos, son\textquotedblright{} — the two plural forms you now hold
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ustedes son\textquotedblright{}, addressing a group
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}they are\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Son}.) What did Latin's \emph{sunt} lose? (Its \textbf{-t}, like every other final \emph{-t}.) Who else does \emph{son} address? (\textbf{Ustedes}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sois]{sois — the last of the six}

\label{lesson:ES-C09-sois}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}they are.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Son}.) And which region uses \emph{vosotros}? (\emph{Spain}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one syllable, and the paradigm closes}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{vosotros sois} — \emph{you all are}, in Spain.
\end{quote}

One syllable, and with it the six forms of \emph{ser} are complete: \emph{soy}, \emph{eres}, \emph{es}, \emph{somos}, \emph{sois}, \emph{son}.

As before, this is the form you need in order to \textbf{follow} Spain rather than to speak everywhere. In the Americas, \emph{ustedes son} does the same job.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin had \textbf{estis}. Spanish wore away the \emph{e-} at the front and the \emph{-t-} in the middle, and \emph{sois} is what was left — a word reduced almost to nothing but still doing its whole job.

That is the pattern with this verb throughout. \emph{Ser} is short everywhere because it is said constantly, and constant use grinds words down. The commonest verb in a language is almost always its most eroded one.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU HEAR: \textquotedblleft{}sois\textquotedblright{}{]} $\to$ Spain, addressing friends.
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}ustedes son\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}vosotros sois\textquotedblright{} — the same sentence, two continents
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the \emph{vosotros} form of \emph{ser}? (\textbf{Sois}.) What Latin word is it worn from? (\textbf{Estis}.) And why is this verb so short everywhere? (Because it is said \textbf{constantly}, and constant use grinds words down.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Review — all of ser}

\label{lesson:ES-C09-repaso-ser}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new. Say \textquotedblleft{}we are\textquotedblright{}, then \textquotedblleft{}they are.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the table, and why it looks like that}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{who} & \textbf{\emph{ser} $\to$} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{soy} \\
tú & \textbf{eres} \\
él · ella · usted & \textbf{es} \\
nosotros & \textbf{somos} \\
vosotros & \textbf{sois} \\
ellos · ustedes & \textbf{son} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Most books present this as a table to memorise. You have built it a form at a time, and you can now read something off it that memorisation would never give you.

\textbf{Five of the six begin with \emph{s-}. One does not.} \emph{Eres} is the outlier, and it is the outlier because it comes from somewhere else — Latin \emph{eris}, from \emph{esse}'s own future stem, pulled in to fill a gap. The rest are the \emph{s-} family: \emph{sum}, \emph{sumus}, \emph{sunt}.

So the \textquotedblleft{}irregularity\textquotedblright{} is not chaos. It is a seam between two verbs, and you can see exactly where it runs.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all six, top to bottom
  \item the five \emph{s-} forms, then \emph{eres} on its own
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give all six forms of \emph{ser}. (\emph{Soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son}.) How many begin with \emph{s-}? (\textbf{Five}.) And why does the sixth not? (It came from a \textbf{different Latin verb} — the seam is visible.)
\end{tcolorbox}
